steps.title: Drive resolution
steps.body: At two metres a minute a hydraulic drive runs on a very small fraction of full flow, the least linear part of a proportional valve's characteristic. Add seal friction and you get stick-slip: the motor holds, breaks free, holds again. On deck it looks like a slight shudder. On the record it is periodic noise at a frequency that has nothing to do with the water column.
points: A closed-loop electric drive with position feedback holds low speed more precisely
Which is much of why research vessels specify electric — not because it is better in general, but because it is better there

steps.title: Level wind placement and reversal
steps.body: At speed a level wind has momentum on its side and the rope more or less falls where it should. At two metres a minute the rope has to be actively placed, turn by turn, and every mechanism's backlash shows up as a small lateral hesitation.
points: The moment that matters is the reversal at the flange, where the level wind changes direction and the rope steps across
Done with slop it puts a tension transient into the cable at every flange, once per wrap, for the whole cast
Which is precisely the kind of periodic artefact that survives into a processed record

steps.title: Layer change
steps.body: As the drum fills, effective radius grows and line pull and speed change with it. What is less discussed is the transition: the moment the rope steps up a layer, effective radius changes abruptly rather than smoothly.
points: At working speeds that transient is lost in the noise
At two metres a minute it is a visible step in tension — and if you are holding a sensor at a fixed altitude, a step in altitude

cta.body: Minimum controllable line speed, level wind behaviour through the reversal, and how cable out is derived. If you are writing a survey winch specification, those are the lines we would want to see — send us what you have and we will tell you what is missing.

frontmatter.lede: Six questions. Some of the answers point away from buying anything from us, which is rather the point.

faqs.q: What is the drum and shaft condition?
faqs.a: These are the expensive structural elements. Sound drum and shaft, and refurbishment is almost always the better answer. Significant wear or cracking in either and the economics change quickly.

faqs.q: What state are the brakes and hydraulics in?
faqs.a: Both are renewable. Neither should decide the outcome on its own — but a hydraulic system that has been contaminated for years tells you something about how the machine has been run.

If the work you are winning now needs more depth, more load or better control than the machine was built for, an upgrade during rebuild may get you there. Sometimes it will not, and that is a genuine reason to replace.

Obsolete control systems are the commonest reason a sound machine is uneconomic. If the electronics cannot be supported, the rebuild has to include replacing them — which is often still cheaper than a new machine, but changes the sum.
Where the equipment sits in its certification cycle affects both cost and timing. A rebuild that coincides with a renewal survey is more efficient than one that does not.

faqs.q: How long do you need it for?
faqs.a: Three more years and five more years are different decisions. Be honest about the vessel's own remaining life — there is no sense putting a twenty-year machine into a hull with five years left.

cta.heading: Get the questions answered properly
cta.body: A condition assessment turns these six questions into a written recommendation with numbers attached.
